Automation

Ray Serve for the model, GitHub Actions for everything around it.

Who this is for

  • You deploy by SSHing somewhere and restarting a process.
  • Retraining happens when someone remembers.
  • You have a CI file that runs tests, and nothing else is automated.

By the end you can

  • Serve a model with replicas, autoscaling and batching you did not implement
  • Compose several models behind one endpoint
  • Write a workflow that can fail, and therefore protects something
  • Automate retraining without eventually shipping a worse model

Companion notebook: automation_tutorial.ipynb.

Two halves of one problem

Ray Serve — the runtime

  • replicas, and routing between them
  • autoscaling on load
  • dynamic batching
  • several models, one endpoint

Answers: how does the model run?

GitHub Actions — the pipeline

  • checks on every pull request
  • retraining on a schedule
  • a quality gate before promotion
  • build, push, deploy

Answers: how does it get there?

Sessions 3 and 4 produced a container that serves one model. This session is what happens when you need ten replicas, three models, and a Monday-morning retrain.

Crash course — the words in this session

WordWhat it means
deploymenta class Ray Serve runs for you and puts behind an HTTP address.
replicaone running copy of that class. Three replicas = three processes answering the same URL, so one slow request does not block the rest.
autoscalingletting Serve add and remove replicas based on load, instead of you picking a number and hoping.
batchingcollecting requests that arrive at the same moment and running them through the model in one call — usually the biggest single speed win.
workflowon the CI side: a YAML file GitHub runs for you on a push, a pull request, or a schedule.
gatea step in that workflow that can fail, and therefore blocks the thing after it. A check that cannot fail protects nothing.

PART 01Ray Serve

A managed pool of actors, with HTTP.

What Serve actually manages

Serve's own architecture

A controller starts and watches everything, a proxy takes the HTTP in, and your class runs in replicas.

Read it as "what did I not write?" Your code is only the green boxes.

A deployment is a class

An ordinary class with two decorators: one says how many copies to run, the other lets it speak HTTP through FastAPI.

@serve.deployment(num_replicas=2, ray_actor_options={"num_cpus": 1})
@serve.ingress(api)                    # it speaks FastAPI -- same as session 3
class ChurnService:
    def __init__(self, artifact="model.joblib"):
        self.bundle = joblib.load(artifact)     # once per replica, at startup

    @api.post("/predict")
    def predict(self, c: Customer):
        ...

serve.run(ChurnService.bind(), name="churn", route_prefix="/churn")
PartWhat it does
@serve.deployment(num_replicas=2)how many copies of this class to keep alive, each in its own process
ray_actor_options={"num_cpus": 1}what one replica is allowed; Serve uses it to decide what fits where
@serve.ingress(api)mount a FastAPI app on this class — the routes and Pydantic models from session 3, unchanged
__init__runs once per replica, so the model is loaded N times, not per request
.bind()describe the deployment and its arguments without building it; Serve builds it
route_prefixthe path the whole application answers under
requests answered per replica pid: {1803995: 31, 1803990: 29}

Measured: 60 requests, two distinct process ids. You declared num_replicas=2; you did not write a load balancer, a health check or a restart loop.

And validation still comes from Pydantic — a bad request is 422, exactly as in session 3. The contract does not change when the runtime does.

A deployment is a class — part by part

The deployment, one decorator at a time. Press m to hold it still.

Autoscaling and batching, as configuration

Both are settings, not code you write. You state the range of replicas and the load you want each to carry.

@serve.deployment(autoscaling_config={
    "min_replicas": 1,
    "max_replicas": 4,
    "target_ongoing_requests": 5,      # scale out past this
})

@serve.batch(max_batch_size=32, batch_wait_timeout_s=0.02)
async def score_many(self, rows: list):
    # Serve collects concurrent calls into ONE list, so the model runs once
    return [float(p) for p in self.model.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame(rows))[:, 1]]
PartWhat it does
min_replicas / max_replicasthe range it may scale inside — the floor is what absorbs the first burst
target_ongoing_requeststhe load per replica it aims for; above it, add one
@serve.batch(max_batch_size=32)collect concurrent calls into one list and run the model once
batch_wait_timeout_s=0.02how long to wait for a batch to fill — the latency you trade for throughput
async defit has to be async: the method is handed a list of arguments and returns a list of results

Session 3 measured that batching was 87× cheaper per customer — but you had to expose a batch endpoint and the caller had to use it. @serve.batch gets the same benefit from callers that keep sending one row at a time.

The trade-off is latency. batch_wait_timeout_s is how long a request may wait for company. Too high and quiet periods feel slow.

Composition — three deployments, one endpoint

One deployment holding handles to two others. Callers see a single URL; behind it, two models run and their answers are combined.

@serve.deployment
class Router:
    def __init__(self, risk, value):
        self.risk, self.value = risk, value        # handles to other deployments

    async def __call__(self, request):
        f = await request.json()
        r = await self.risk.remote(f)               # may run on another node
        v = await self.value.remote(f)
        return {"action": "call now" if r > .5 and v > .4 else "monitor"}

serve.run(Router.bind(RiskModel.bind(), ValueModel.bind()), route_prefix="/composed")
POST /composed -> 200 {'risk': 0.8, 'value': 0.75, 'action': 'call now'}
PartWhat it does
.bind(RiskModel.bind(), ValueModel.bind())handles are passed in, so the router never imports the models
await self.risk.remote(f)a call to another deployment, which may be on another machine
two awaitsthey run on their own replicas, so the slow one does not wait for the other to be written
one route_prefixthe caller sees one URL; scaling each model separately is your business, not theirs

Each part scales independently. If the risk model is expensive and the value model is cheap, give them different replica counts — something a single monolithic service cannot do.

A class passed to @serve.ingress may not define __call__ — ingress is for FastAPI-routed classes, __call__ for raw requests. Mixing them fails at deploy time.

PART 02GitHub Actions

Start with the check, not the deployment.

The workflow file, part by part

A workflow is a YAML file GitHub runs for you. This is its head.

name: validate
# when GitHub runs it
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  decks-and-notebooks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
PartWhat it does
name:what the run is called in the Actions tab
on:the events: every push to main, every pull request, and a button
jobs:a job is one machine. This file has one, named by you
runs-on:a clean rented VM; nothing from your laptop is on it
steps:run in order, and the first one that fails stops the job
uses:a ready-made action, pinned to @v4, never @main

The first check, in full

      - name: every deck must be balanced and offline
        run: |
          python - <<'PY'
          import glob, re, sys
          bad = []
          for f in glob.glob("*/*_slides.html"):
              t = open(f).read()
              if t.count("<section") != t.count("</section>"):
                  bad.append(f"{f}: unbalanced sections")
              # src, not href: a deck must carry its own pictures, but the reading list
              # at the end is allowed to link out to the docs it recommends
              ext = re.findall(r'src="(?!#|data:)[^"]+"', t)
              if ext:
                  bad.append(f"{f}: external reference {ext[:2]}")
              print(f"{f}: {t.count('<section')} slides")
          if bad:
              print("FAILURES:", *bad, sep="\n  "); sys.exit(1)
          PY
LineMeaning
run: | and <<'PY'one shell script; it pipes the lines up to PY into Python
glob(...)every deck in the repository, whatever the session is called
the tag countsa deck that lost a closing tag swallows the slide after it
re.findall(...)a picture that is not embedded; it would vanish offline
print per fileso the log says what was checked, not only what broke
bad then exit(1)report every problem at once, then fail the job

The second check, in full

      - name: every notebook must be valid and carry its outputs
        run: |
          python - <<'PY'
          import glob, json, sys
          bad = []
          for f in glob.glob("*/*_tutorial.ipynb"):
              nb = json.load(open(f))
              code = [c for c in nb["cells"] if c["cell_type"] == "code"]
              errs = [o for c in nb["cells"] for o in c.get("outputs", [])
                      if o.get("output_type") == "error"]
              if errs:
                  bad.append(f"{f}: {len(errs)} stored error outputs")
              print(f"{f}: {len(nb['cells'])} cells, {len(code)} code, {len(errs)} errors")
          if bad:
              print("FAILURES:", *bad, sep="\n  "); sys.exit(1)
          PY

A notebook is JSON, so json.load alone catches a file damaged in a merge. The rest looks for one thing: a cell that stored an error output.

The last two checks

      - name: the course index must link every built session
        run: |
          python - <<'PY'
          import glob, os, re, sys
          readme = open("README.md").read()
          missing = [d for d in sorted(glob.glob("*/"))
                     if glob.glob(os.path.join(d, "*_slides.html"))
                     and f"({d.rstrip('/')})" not in readme]
          print("unlinked sessions:", missing or "none")
          sys.exit(1 if missing else 0)
          PY

      - name: the example in the notebook must be the file that runs
        run: |
          python - <<'PY'
          import json, sys
          nb = json.load(open("11-automation/automation_tutorial.ipynb"))
          cell = next(c for c in nb["cells"]
                      if "".join(c["source"]).startswith("%%writefile ci-example.yml"))
          taught = "".join(cell["source"]).split("\n", 1)[1].strip()
          live = open(".github/workflows/validate.yml").read().strip()
          print("the notebook example and the live workflow agree:", taught == live)
          sys.exit(0 if taught == live else 1)
          PY

The last one guards this very deck: teach one file and run another, and the job goes red.

A check that cannot fail is decoration

if bad:
    print("FAILURES:", *bad, sep="\n  ")
    sys.exit(1)                    # non-zero fails the job. This line is the point.
ConceptMeaning
on:which events trigger it — push, PR, schedule, manual
runs-on:a clean machine; nothing from your laptop is present
uses:a prebuilt action, pinned — @v4, never @main
secrets.* / vars.*secrets are masked in logs; variables are not
exit codenon-zero fails the job. Everything else is a suggestion

The failure mode to avoid: a job that prints warnings and exits 0. It stays green for a year while the thing it was supposed to check quietly rots.

Where you see green or red

Where to lookWhat it tells you
the Actions tab of the repositoryevery run, newest first; open one and each step has its own log
beside the commit, on the code pagea tick, a red cross, or a yellow dot while it is still running
on a pull requestthe checks box — this is the thing that keeps a broken branch out of main
your inboxGitHub mails you when a run on main fails
gh run list                     # the recent runs, with their conclusion
gh run watch                    # follow the one in flight
gh run view --log-failed        # only the step that broke, and why

A step that fails ends its log with Process completed with exit code 1 and turns the job red. That line is the sys.exit(1) from the slide before, arriving at GitHub.

Retraining: the part everyone forgets

The full quality gate, line by line

The step that can say no. It compares the new model's score against the one in production and exits non-zero if it is worse.

- name: refuse to promote a worse model
  run: |
    python - <<'PY'
    import json, sys
    new  = json.load(open("metrics.json"))
    base = json.load(open("baseline.json"))
    delta = new["roc_auc"] - base["roc_auc"]
    print(f"new {new['roc_auc']:.4f} baseline {base['roc_auc']:.4f} delta {delta:+.4f}")
    if delta < -0.005:
        print("REFUSING to promote: the new model is worse."); sys.exit(1)
    PY

Ten lines between "trained" and "shipped".

Without it, a Monday cron will eventually promote a worse model — because data drifts, an upstream column changes, or a bug slips in. The first person to notice is a customer, three weeks later.

Automation does not remove human error. It removes the human who would have caught it — unless you encode what that human was checking.

The other five lines that make it safe

LineWithout it
concurrency: {group: retrain}two retrains race; one overwrites the other's model
environment: productionno human sees the change before customers do
permissions: id-token: writelong-lived cloud keys sitting in repo secrets
dvc pull at a pinned commit"which data trained this?" has no answer
image tagged ${{ github.sha }}you cannot roll back to a specific commit
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 3 * * 1"          # 03:00 UTC Monday. Note: UTC, always.
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      reason: {description: why are you retraining by hand?, required: true}

Where the whole course meets

            push / schedule
                  |
          GitHub Actions
                  |
   session 6  dvc pull            # which data
   session 1  train (leak-proof)  # honest metric
   session 7  log to MLflow       # which run
      GATE    refuse if worse     # the ten lines above

Cheat sheet

# Ray Serve
@serve.deployment(num_replicas=2, autoscaling_config={...})
@serve.ingress(fastapi_app)              # no __call__ in the same class
@serve.batch(max_batch_size=32, batch_wait_timeout_s=0.02)
serve.run(App.bind(Dep1.bind(), Dep2.bind()), name="x", route_prefix="/x")
serve.status().applications ; serve.delete("x") ; serve.shutdown()

# GitHub Actions
on: {push: {branches:[main]}, pull_request: , schedule: [{cron: "0 3 * * 1"}]}
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
uses: actions/checkout@v4 | actions/setup-python@v5
concurrency: {group: retrain, cancel-in-progress: false}
permissions: {contents: read, id-token: write}
environment: production                  # attach a required reviewer
sys.exit(1)                              # the only thing that actually fails a job
${{ secrets.X }}  ${{ vars.Y }}  ${{ github.sha }}

Start tomorrow, in this order

  1. Write the CI job that would have caught your last broken merge. Make sure it can fail.
  2. Add concurrency to anything that writes shared state.
  3. If you retrain on a schedule, add the gate today. Ten lines.
  4. Put the git SHA in the image tag, so a rollback is a tag rather than an investigation.
  5. Only then reach for Serve autoscaling — replicas are easy, and a bad model shipping automatically is not.
